name: Lemon juice / baking soda on scars

lead: This home remedy involves rubbing lemon juice, baking soda (sodium bicarbonate) or a paste of the two on scars so they look paler and smoother.
Believers point to lemon juice's acidity as a lightener and baking soda's abrasiveness as an exfoliant. No studies were found testing this practice for scars.

paras: It is mixed at home and applied to the scar for a short time before rinsing, repeated over days or weeks. Users often combine it with other home skin routines.

Wikipedia describes phytophotodermatitis, a reaction to plant furanocoumarins (found in citrus such as lime) combined with UV-A light, producing redness, burning and blisters within about 48 hours and pigment marks that can persist for years. Sodium bicarbonate is listed as causing serious eye irritation.

angle.text: Lemon juice and baking soda pastes are used at home in the hope of lightening the surface of a scar so it looks paler. The practice circulates by word of mouth, and no clinical studies were found. Citrus juice on skin in sunlight is a known cause of dark marks and blistering.

lead: Applying lemon juice, baking soda or a paste of both to scars is a do-it-yourself practice that circulates as a way to lighten or smooth scars. No clinical studies of the practice were found in the sources reviewed.

Related reference material documents risks. Phytophotodermatitis is a skin inflammation triggered by contact with light-sensitising plant compounds, notably furanocoumarins, followed by UV-A exposure; lime is among the best-known citrus triggers, and the reaction can leave hyperpigmented marks lasting for years [1]. Sodium bicarbonate solutions are mildly alkaline, and the compound is listed as causing serious eye irritation [2].

paras: The practice uses common kitchen ingredients. Lemon juice is acidic and sodium bicarbonate is mildly alkaline in solution and has mild abrasive properties [2]. Neither has been established as a scar treatment in the sources reviewed.

Phytophotodermatitis typically begins within 24 hours of contact and peaks at 48 to 72 hours, with redness, itching, burning and possible blisters; furanocoumarins can trigger melanin production, leaving black, brown or purplish marks that may persist for several years [1]. Citrus such as lime is a well-known cause [1].
Wikipedia's sodium bicarbonate article does not discuss cosmetic exfoliation or give skin-irritation data, but lists serious eye irritation as the main hazard [2].
